general.q: How much does it cost to paint a room in the Twin Cities?
general.a: For a standard bedroom with 8-foot ceilings, walls only, most homeowners in the west metro land somewhere in the $400–$510 range for labor. Trim, ceilings, tall or vaulted walls, heavy patching, and dark-over-light color changes all push it up. The honest answer is that nobody can price your room accurately from a website — that is what the free estimate is for. See how I put a number together.

general.q: Do you really have me buy the paint?
general.a:
Yes, and it saves you money. Painting companies typically mark paint up 30–50%. When you buy it directly you pay store price, you pick the exact brand and sheen you want, and you keep the leftovers for touch-ups later.

You will not be guessing. After the walkthrough I give you an exact list — brand, product line, sheen, color, and how many gallons — so you buy the right thing once. If you would rather not deal with the store, tell me and we will work something out.

general.q: How long does painting a room take?
general.a: A single bedroom, walls only, is usually one day. Add trim and doors and it is typically two. A whole main floor is normally three to five days depending on how much patching and how many colors are involved. I will give you a realistic day count in your estimate, and if something changes I will tell you before it becomes a surprise.

general.q: Do I need to move my furniture out?
general.a: No. Move small, fragile, and valuable things yourself — electronics, art, anything you would hate to lose. I will move the rest to the middle of the room, cover it, and cover the floors. Everything goes back where it was before I leave.

general.q: You are 19. Why should I trust you with my house?
general.a:
Fair question, and I would rather answer it than dodge it. I have been painting since I was young — on job sites, on crews, doing the prep and the cut-in and the cleanup that nobody sees. What you are hiring is the hands that do the work, not a salesperson who hands your house to whoever is available that week.

Here is how I would suggest you protect yourself with any painter: ask for a written estimate, do not pay in full up front, and walk the finished job with them before the final payment. I do all three by default. More about who I am and how I work.

I am based in Plymouth and work across the west metro — Maple Grove, Minnetonka, Wayzata, Golden Valley, Medina, New Hope, Crystal, Osseo, Orono, St. Louis Park, and the surrounding suburbs. See the full service area. If you are just outside it, ask anyway.

extra.q: How do I get an estimate?
extra.a: Call or text (952) 486-0205, or send the form. I will get back to you, usually the same day, to set a time to come look at the space. The visit takes about 20 minutes. You get a written number, and there is no charge and no obligation.

extra.q: Do you give estimates over the phone?
extra.a: I can give you a rough range over the phone or from photos, and I am happy to. But I will not pretend it is a real quote. Wall condition, patching, ceiling height, and color changes move the number a lot, and I would rather see it than guess and be wrong in either direction.

extra.q: How much prep work do you actually do?
extra.a: Prep is most of the job and it is where cheap paint jobs fall apart. On a normal interior repaint that means: furniture moved and covered, floors covered, outlet and switch plates off, nail holes and dings filled and sanded smooth, glossy or stained spots spot-primed, and every edge cut in by hand. Caulk lines get touched up where trim meets wall. Then the paint goes on.

Two coats, unless we agree otherwise for a specific reason. One coat over an existing similar color can look fine on the day and then show flashing and roller lap marks in a year. If your estimate says two coats, that is what you get.

extra.q: What if I do not like the color once it is on the wall?
extra.a: Color always reads differently on a wall than on a chip — that is normal, not a mistake. Buy a sample pot first and paint a two-foot square on the actual wall, then look at it in morning light and at night. I will tell you honestly if I think a color is going to fight the room. If you change your mind after a coat is on, repainting is additional work and I will quote it before doing it.

Yes. Flat ceiling paint, water-stain sealing, and refreshing ceilings that have yellowed. I do not spray or scrape popcorn texture — textured ceilings in older homes can contain materials that need a certified abatement contractor, and that is not work I take on. More about ceiling painting.

Not right now. Cabinet refinishing done properly needs a spray setup and a controlled space, and I would rather tell you no than hand you a brushed cabinet job that chips in a year. Interior walls, ceilings, trim, and doors are what I do.
No — interior only. Keeping the focus narrow is deliberate. It means the work I do take on gets done properly instead of squeezed between three other kinds of jobs.

Nail holes, dings, small dents, popped screws, and minor patches are part of a normal repaint and I handle them. Large holes, water damage, ceiling repairs, or anything structural is a different trade and I will tell you that up front rather than paint over it. More on what I patch.

No deposit on small jobs. On larger projects I may ask for a deposit to reserve the dates, with the balance due when the job is finished and you have walked it with me and you are happy. Cash, check, Venmo, and Zelle all work. You get it in writing before anything starts.
Saturdays, yes. Sundays I do not work — that day is for church and family. I would rather be upfront about that than be vague and cancel on you.

extra.q: What happens if something gets damaged?
extra.a: Tell me right away and I will make it right. That is exactly why I cover floors and furniture before anything opens, and why we walk the finished job together before you pay the balance.

extra.q: Will there be a strong paint smell?
extra.a: Much less than it used to be. Modern interior latex paints are low-VOC and the smell is usually gone within a day with normal ventilation. If anyone in the house is sensitive, or there is a baby or someone with asthma, tell me and I will recommend a zero-VOC product for your list.

It depends on the season. Spring and fall book up fastest in the Twin Cities; January through March is usually the easiest time to get on the calendar and the quietest time to have someone in your house. Ask and I will tell you honestly what is open.

I want to give you a straight answer instead of a marketing one: True Painting MN is a new business and I am in the process of getting general liability coverage in place. Until I can tell you it is done, I am not going to claim it. If insurance is a requirement for your job — and for some homeowners and most HOAs it is — ask me directly and I will tell you exactly where I stand at that moment.

extra.q: Do you paint homes built before 1978?
extra.a: Ask me before you book. Homes built before 1978 can have lead-based paint underneath, and federal law puts specific requirements on contractors who disturb it. I will not cut corners on that or pretend the rule does not apply. Tell me the age of your home when you call and I will tell you straight whether I can take the job.

interior.q: How many coats will my walls need?
interior.a: Two, on almost every job. Going from a dark color to a light one, or covering a strong red or deep blue, may need a primer coat first — I will tell you that at the estimate rather than discovering it halfway through and asking for more money.

interior.q: Should I paint the ceiling and trim at the same time?
interior.a: If you are on the fence, yes. Adding ceiling or trim to a room that is already covered, taped, and set up costs far less than coming back to do it as its own job later. Fresh walls also have a way of making old trim look worse than you remembered.

interior.q: What sheen should I use on walls?
interior.a: For most Twin Cities homes: eggshell or matte in bedrooms and living rooms, and satin in kitchens, bathrooms, mudrooms, and hallways where walls get wiped down. Flat hides wall imperfections best but does not clean well. I will put the right sheen on your paint list.

interior.q: Can you paint one accent wall?
interior.a: Yes, and it is one of the cheapest ways to change how a room feels. It is a small job, so it often makes sense to pair it with another room you were already thinking about.

ceiling.q: Do you paint over water stains?
ceiling.a: Only after the leak is fixed and the area is dry, and only with a stain-blocking primer first. Regular ceiling paint over a water stain will let the stain bleed right back through within weeks.

ceiling.q: Do you spray or roll ceilings?
ceiling.a: I roll. Spraying is faster but requires masking off the entire room, and in an occupied home rolling gives a cleaner, more controlled result with far less overspray risk to your floors and furniture.

ceiling.q: Can you paint a popcorn or textured ceiling?
ceiling.a: I do not scrape or remove popcorn texture. Textured ceilings installed before the mid-1980s can contain asbestos and that is work for a licensed abatement contractor, not a painter. If your textured ceiling is sound and just needs paint, ask me and we will talk about whether it is a good candidate.

trim.q: Can you paint stained wood trim white?
trim.a: Yes, and it is one of the biggest visual changes you can make to a 1980s or 1990s house. It is real work — the trim has to be cleaned, scuff-sanded, and primed with a bonding primer before any finish coat, or the paint will peel off the varnish. Expect it to cost meaningfully more than repainting already-painted trim, and expect the result to be worth it.

trim.q: What sheen is best for trim and doors?
trim.a: Semi-gloss for most homes — it wipes clean and gives trim definition against the wall. Satin is a softer, more modern look that hides imperfections in older trim better. Either is fine; I will show you the difference.

trim.q: Do you paint doors on or off the hinges?
trim.a: Usually on, with hardware removed and the edges done carefully. Taking doors off gives a slightly better finish but leaves you without doors for a day, which most families do not want. I will tell you which makes sense for your house.

drywall.q: What counts as a small repair?
drywall.a: Nail and screw holes, anchor holes, dings from furniture, small dents, popped drywall screws, hairline settling cracks, and patches up to roughly the size of your hand. These are normal parts of a repaint and are usually included.

drywall.q: What will you not take on?
drywall.a: Large holes, water-damaged drywall, ceiling replacement, texture matching across a whole ceiling, and anything involving structure, plumbing, or mold. I will tell you plainly that you need a drywall or restoration contractor first rather than painting over a problem.

On a smooth wall, yes — patched, sanded flush, primed, and painted, and you will not find it. On a heavily textured wall, a good patch blends closely but a textured surface is never a perfect match. I will set that expectation before I start, not after.

pricing.q: Why is your price lower than the big companies?
pricing.a: Less overhead, not less work. There is no office, no sales commission, no branded truck fleet, and no crew coordinator taking a cut. You are also buying the paint directly rather than paying a markup on it. The prep and the number of coats do not change.

pricing.q: Do you charge by the hour or by the job?
pricing.a: By the job. You get one written number before I start, and that is the number, unless you add work or we find something behind the furniture that neither of us knew about — in which case I stop and talk to you before doing anything extra.
Yes. Free to get, free to think about, and free to say no to. I will not follow up more than once.

pricing.q: What makes a quote go up?
pricing.a: Tall or vaulted ceilings, lots of trim and doors, dark-to-light color changes, heavy patching, stained trim that needs bonding primer, and rooms that are hard to set up in. What brings it down: doing several rooms at once, walls only, and keeping a similar color.
